facts.claim: Lee DeWyze wrote "Blackbird Song" for AMC's The Walking Dead. It was used in Season 4, Episode 13, "Alone".
Qobuz credits Lee DeWyze as composer/lyricist, producer, and mixer of the track. It lists the track at 4:14 and the label as Vanguard Records (Welk Music Group).
DeWyze came up with the idea of writing a song for the series after it had run a few seasons. He had not been interested in watching it in its early days.
DeWyze wrote the song in his living room and finished it over two evenings.
DeWyze wrote the song without any guarantee it would be used. He pushed Welk Music Group's Fred Jasper, VP of TV/Film Licensing, to submit it to the show.
The song plays at the beginning and end of "Alone", for about four minutes of airtime in total. It soundtracks a flashback to Bob Stookey's solitary wandering before he joined Rick's group.
"Alone" aired on AMC on March 9, 2014. The song debuted at number 29 on Billboard's Pop Digital Songs chart and appears on The Walking Dead (AMC Original Soundtrack), Vol. 2.
One reviewer describes the track as heavy on acoustic guitar and violin, with DeWyze's vocals as the centerpiece.
DeWyze performed the song live at The Ark in Ann Arbor, MI, in July 2014.

DeWyze won American Idol season 9 on May 26, 2010. Before that he had released two independent albums, So I'm Told (2007) and Slumberland (2010). He is from Mount Prospect, Illinois, and his influences include Cat Stevens, Eric Clapton, Ben Harper, and Simon & Garfunkel.

research.lineage: Acoustic, folk-leaning singer-songwriter material written for a TV drama, from an American Idol winner who had earlier released independent albums.

draft:
The first thing **Blackbird Song** gives you isn't a word. Over a slow, fingerpicked run of acoustic guitar chords, Lee DeWyze holds a long, wordless "ooh," low and breathy, with just a slight tremble of vibrato at the edges. Only after that hum does the song start speaking, and by then the mood is set: someone is about to say something hard, and gently.

What follows is barely a lyric sheet, eight lines with a refrain doing most of the work. The instruction comes first: pack up, get out, the blackbird song is over. Then a set of images flickers past like a town seen through a car window: dry mouths, a running river, "Hands are tied, preacher sighs." That last image is the bleakest thing here. Even the person whose job is comfort has nothing left to offer but a breath.

Then the song turns. "Don't be scared, I'm still here," DeWyze sings, and right behind it, "No more time for crying dear." Both lines are love, and they pull against each other. One holds a hand. The other wipes a face a little too fast. It's the voice of someone who has decided grief is a luxury the moment can't afford. Is the narrator steadying the other person, or steadying themselves by saying it out loud? The song never settles it, and DeWyze's delivery doesn't push either way. The voice stays close and upfront, unhurried, never rising to plead.

DeWyze wrote it for The Walking Dead, a show he admits he hadn't cared about in its early seasons, and he wrote it on spec in his living room over two evenings, with no promise it would be used. He pushed his label's licensing VP, Fred Jasper, to submit it anyway. It landed in Season 4's "Alone," opening and closing the episode over a flashback to Bob Stookey wandering by himself before he found Rick's group. That pairing sharpens the lyric. "I'm still here" means something different laid over a man with no one around to say it to him.

DeWyze won American Idol, but this is closer to the records he says shaped him, Cat Stevens and Simon & Garfunkel, than to anything built for a stage. He produced and mixed it himself, and on this ballad that restraint is the right call: guitar, a voice, no harmonies to soften the blow.

It sticks because it sounds like the calmest person in a bad situation, the one telling you to leave while making sure you know you're not leaving alone.
